The teen put an object under his shirt and told his mother around the time she phoned 9-1-1 that he was going to say he had a gun, said New York Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly. The teen told her, " 'I'm prepared to die,' " Kelly told reporters. When authorities arrived at the Bedford-Stuyvesant apartment, the teenager had something stuffed under his shirt and several times showed a knife to police. "Shoot me, kill me," he shouted, according to Kelly. "Come get me. I have a gun. Let's do this." Coppin ignored repeated commands to stop and get on the ground. Witnesses said the teen appeared to be holding an object underneath his shirt and pointed it at the officers. Coppin continued to approach officers, as they ordered him to stop, said Kelly. Twenty shots were fired; Coppin was struck eight times, Kelly said. "This was a terrible tragedy for Khiel's family, no doubt about it," said Kelly. But the commissioner stressed that officers reasonably believed they were about to receive fire. Kelly said the teen's mother reported he had not taken his anti-depressant and anti-psychotic medication. Police have not recovered a gun and do not believe that Coppin was armed, Kelly said. A reporter asked Kelly if it's possible the young man was goading police to shoot him, a phenomenon known commonly in law enforcement circles as suicide-by-cop. Coppin was taken to a hospital where he was declared dead. An autopsy is scheduled for Tuesday, the medical examiner's office said. The Rev. Police said they were investigating whether Coppin had a history of mental illness and whether his mother had tried to have him hospitalized earlier Monday. The shooting came a year after unarmed groom Sean Bell, 23, was killed hours before his wedding in a shooting involving New York police. In 1999, unarmed African immigrant Amadou Diallo, 22, died when police in the Bronx shot him 19 times. Bystander Dyshawn Gibson described Monday's shooting to CNN affiliate WABC-TV. **NEW YORK (CNN)** — An 18-year-old man carrying a hairbrush was fatally shot Monday night in a hail of gunfire from New York City police officers. Following the tragedy, the victim’s brother, Joel Coppin, briefly addressed reporters, demanding, "We want justice."

According to authorities, officers were responding to a 911 call placed by Khiel Coppin’s mother regarding a "family dispute with a gun." NYPD Deputy Commissioner Paul Browne stated that during the recording—played at a news conference Tuesday—Coppin could be heard shouting in the background, "I've got a gun, I've got a gun." New York Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly added that around the time of the call, the teenager placed an object beneath his shirt, informed his mother that he intended to claim he was armed, and told her, "'I'm prepared to die.'"

Upon arriving at the Bedford-Stuyvesant apartment, officers encountered Coppin with something concealed under his shirt. Kelly reported that the teenager repeatedly displayed a knife toward officers while yelling, "Shoot me, kill me... Come get me. I have a gun. Let's do this." 

Coppin ignored repeated police commands to halt and get on the ground. Witnesses confirmed that he appeared to hold an object beneath his clothing, pointing it directly at the officers as he continued to advance. 

Officers fired 20 rounds, striking Coppin eight times. "This was a terrible tragedy for Khiel's family, no doubt about it," Kelly remarked, while emphasizing that the responding officers reasonably believed they were under imminent threat of gunfire. Kelly also noted that Coppin's mother reported her son had not taken his prescribed antidepressant and antipsychotic medications.

Investigators found no firearm at the scene and do not believe Coppin was armed. When asked by a reporter whether the young man may have intentionally provoked the officers—a phenomenon known in law enforcement as "suicide-by-cop"—Kelly conceded, "That's certainly a possibility."

Witnesses and neighbors provided starkly different accounts of the encounter. "The boy didn't have no gun, he had a brush on him," said neighbor Andre Wildman, who witnessed the shooting. Another resident, Wayne Holder, argued that law enforcement should face stricter requirements before employing lethal force: "At least see a gun before you start to discharge it," Holder stated, adding critically that police "don't even have to see it, [if] they think you got one, you're going to get shot." Bystander Dyshawn Gibson, speaking to CNN affiliate WABC-TV, recalled a non-threatening sequence: "He dropped the brush," Gibson said. "He put his hands up. Police just started firing."

In an initial statement released late Monday, police described Coppin pacing inside the apartment prior to the shooting. "He began screaming from the window at his mother and the police," the statement said. A police spokesman noted that Coppin subsequently climbed out of the window and began crossing the sidewalk toward the officers, at which point police opened fire.

Coppin was rushed to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The medical examiner's office has scheduled an autopsy for Tuesday. 

The Rev. Al Sharpton's National Action Network is expected to hold a news conference Tuesday regarding the incident. Meanwhile, police confirmed they are investigating whether Coppin had a history of mental illness and whether his mother had attempted to have him hospitalized earlier in the day.

The shooting comes exactly one year after the high-profile death of Sean Bell, an unarmed 23-year-old groom killed by police hours before his wedding. It also recalls the 1999 case of Amadou Diallo, an unarmed 22-year-old African immigrant who died after being struck by 19 police bullets in the Bronx.

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — The fatal police shooting of a mentally ill 18-year-old in Brooklyn has re-ignited intense scrutiny over the New York City Police Department's use of deadly force, drawing painful comparisons to some of the city's most infamous police shootings.

Khiel Coppin was shot and killed by police officers outside his Bedford-Stuyvesant home on Monday after he confronted them with an object wrapped in a cloth that officers believed was a firearm. The object was later determined to be a hairbrush.

The tragic sequence of events began shortly after 4:00 p.m., when Coppin's mother, Denise Owens, made a desperate 911 call requesting medical assistance for her son, who suffered from severe mental illness, including schizophrenia.

According to transcripts released by police, Owens told the dispatcher that her son had stopped taking his medication and was acting aggressively. 

"He's acting crazy," Owens told the 911 operator, adding that her son had a knife and was making threats. "He needs to go to the hospital. Please send an ambulance."

However, because the call involved a report of a knife, NYPD patrol officers were dispatched to the scene alongside emergency medical personnel.

### 'I have a gun'

When officers arrived at the residential street in Bed-Stuy, Coppin jumped out of a first-floor window wearing no shirt and holding a black object under a piece of cloth, refusing police commands to stop.

Speaking at a news conference on Tuesday, NYPD Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly defended the officers' immediate perception of a threat while outlining the rapid escalation of the encounter.

"The officers repeatedly ordered him to stop and show his hands," Kelly told reporters. "Instead, Mr. Coppin advanced toward the officers, shouting, 'I have a gun! I'm going to shoot you!' and 'Let's do this!'"

Kelly stated that five officers fired a total of 20 rounds after Coppin rushed toward them, hitting him five times. 

"The officers were faced with a situation where a subject stated he had a weapon, engaged in an aggressive posture, and charged at them with an object thrust forward in a shooting stance," Kelly said. "It was later discovered that the object he held was a hairbrush, not a firearm."

Coppin was rushed to Woodhull Medical and Mental Health Center, where he was pronounced dead.

### Community outrage and witness reactions

The shooting has left the Bedford-Stuyvesant community reeling, with neighbors and relatives questioning why officers used lethal force against a young man known in the neighborhood to be emotionally disturbed.

"They knew he was sick. Everyone on this block knew Khiel had problems," said local resident Marcus Williams, who witnessed the aftermath of the shooting. "His mother called for an ambulance to help him, not for the police to come and execute him in the street."

Coppin's family expressed devastation that a cry for medical help ended in a fatal shooting. "I called for help for my son," Owens said through tears at a community gathering Tuesday night. "He needed help, not bullets."

Bystanders questioned the sheer volume of shots fired by the officers. Witnesses described a barrage of gunfire that shattered the late-afternoon calm of the residential neighborhood.

***

**RELATED LINKS**
* **Archive:** NYPD under scrutiny following Sean Bell shooting
* **Fact Check:** NYPD policies on dealing with emotionally disturbed persons

***

### Echoes of past tragedies

The incident in Bedford-Stuyvesant has reopened deep wounds in a city still grappling with previous high-profile NYPD shootings involving unarmed Black men.

Community advocates and civil rights leaders were quick to compare Coppin's death to the 2006 shooting of Sean Bell, a 23-year-old groom-to-be who was struck by NYPD officers who fired 50 rounds at his car outside a Queens strip club on the morning of his wedding. Bell was unarmed.

The shooting also drew immediate comparisons to the 1999 death of Amadou Diallo, a 22-year-old West African immigrant who was shot 19 times by four police officers in the vestibule of his Bronx apartment building. In that case, officers mistook Diallo's wallet for a gun—a deadly parallel to the hairbrush Coppin was holding on Monday.

Civil rights advocates argue that the NYPD has failed to adequately train officers to de-escalate situations involving mentally ill individuals without resorting to lethal force.

"Once again, we are seeing a tragedy where an unarmed man is killed because officers acted on assumptions rather than de-escalation," said local community activists during a rally outside the 79th Precinct on Tuesday evening. "How many times must a hairbrush or a wallet be mistaken for a gun?"

The Kings County District Attorney's office and the NYPD's Internal Affairs Bureau have launched formal investigations into the shooting. Police Commissioner Kelly emphasized that the department's Force Investigation Division will conduct a thorough review of the incident to determine if proper police protocols were followed.

---
*CNN's Deb Feyerick and Susan Candiotti contributed to this report.*

**MAPLEWOOD, Ohio** — An 18-year-old high school senior remains in critical condition following a police shooting Monday night that occurred while he was experiencing a severe mental health crisis. Authorities later revealed that the weapon the teenager claimed to possess was actually a black hairbrush.

The incident unfolded around 7:45 p.m. in the quiet suburban neighborhood of Oakridge, after family members called 911 requesting medical assistance for 18-year-old Marcus Vance. According to police, the caller stated that Vance was emotionally distraught, making threats to harm himself, and refusing to calm down.

When officers arrived at the scene, Vance was standing in the front yard of his home. According to statement releases and preliminary statements from the Maplewood Police Department, officers attempted to verbally de-escalate the situation from a distance. 

However, police officials say Vance quickly escalated the confrontation. 

"The subject advanced toward the officers while concealing his right hand behind his back," Maplewood Police Chief Robert Sterling said during a Tuesday morning news conference. "He repeatedly shouted that he had a loaded handgun and aggressively warned officers that he was going to open fire. When he abruptly pulled his hand out and pointed a dark object directly at the officers in a shooting stance, two officers discharged their service weapons."

Vance was struck twice in the torso and immediately collapsed. Officers rendered first aid until emergency medical technicians arrived. He was rushed to St. Jude Regional Medical Center, where he underwent emergency surgery and remains in critical but stable condition.

A subsequent search of the scene recovered no firearms. Investigators found only a dark-handled, paddle-style hairbrush lying near Vance where he fell.

Chief Sterling acknowledged the tragic nature of the outcome and noted that state investigators are examining whether the incident was a case of "suicide-by-cop"—a phenomenon in which an individual deliberately behaves in a threatening manner to provoke a lethal response from law enforcement.

"While the investigation is in its early stages, evidence suggests the young man may have intentionally created a scenario where officers felt forced to use deadly force," Sterling said. "Our officers are trained to handle mental health crises, but when presented with what reasonably appears to be an imminent, lethal threat, they must make split-second decisions to protect themselves and the public."

The shooting has left the surrounding neighborhood reeling, with residents expressing a mixture of grief, shock, and anger over how the crisis was handled.

Sarah Jenkins, who lives two doors down from the Vance family, said she watched parts of the encounter from her living room window. 

"I heard shouting, and then three distinct gunshots," Jenkins said, visibly shaken. "Marcus is just a kid. Everyone on this block knows he’s been struggling with depression lately, especially after losing his grandfather earlier this year. He wasn’t a violent person—he was hurting. It breaks my heart that a call for help ended with him being shot."

Another neighbor, David Rivera, questioned whether responding officers used appropriate de-escalation tactics given the nature of the emergency call.

"When a family calls 911 for a mental health emergency, they expect medical help, not a military-style response," Rivera said. "If the family told dispatch he was having a breakdown, why weren't mental health professionals deployed alongside the police? There has to be a better way to handle someone holding a hairbrush."

In response to community concerns, Chief Sterling noted that both officers involved were equipped with body-worn cameras. The footage has been handed over to the State Bureau of Criminal Investigation (BCI), which has taken over the independent inquiry into the shooting.

Per standard department procedure, both officers have been placed on paid administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation. 

The Vance family released a brief statement through their attorney Tuesday afternoon, asking for privacy and requesting prayers for Marcus's recovery, while promising to seek "answers and accountability" for the shooting.

Here is a detailed overview of the November 12, 2007, shooting of 18-year-old Khiel Coppin in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, compiled from contemporary news reports, official NYPD statements, and witness accounts.

---

### **The Incident: November 12, 2007**

On the afternoon of November 12, 2007, Denise Johnston called 911 requesting assistance for her 18-year-old son, Khiel Coppin, who suffered from severe mental illness and was acting aggressively after stopping his medication. 

When NYPD officers arrived at the family’s apartment on Fulton Street in Brooklyn, Coppin had climbed out of a window onto a fire escape, eventually coming down to the street. He had his right hand concealed under a black sweatshirt or shirt draped over his arm, making it appear as though he was concealing a firearm.

Despite repeated orders from officers to stop and show his hands, Coppin advanced toward the police. Five officers opened fire, discharging a total of 20 rounds. Coppin was struck 13 times and died shortly after at Interfaith Medical Center. A subsequent search revealed he was unarmed; the object under his clothing was a black hairbrush.

---

### **Quotes from the Scene and Eyewitnesses**

* **Denise Johnston (Coppin’s Mother):** 
  Johnston had called for medical help, explicitly informing dispatchers that her son had a history of mental illness. Witnesses recalled her distress as the situation escalated. She later publicly criticized the police response:
  > *"I called for help. I didn’t call for them to kill my son. He needed a doctor, not bullets."*

* **Bystanders and Neighbors:**
  Witnesses in the neighborhood described a scene of rapid gunfire and panic. One neighbor told reporters:
  > *"It sounded like firecrackers at first, but then you realized it was gunshots. There were cops everywhere shouting, and then just a hail of bullets."*

---

### **Official Police Statements**

Then-NYPD Police Commissioner Raymond W. Kelly held a press conference shortly after the incident to outline the police department's account of the event and explain why the officers perceived an immediate threat.

* **On the Perception of a Threat:**
  Commissioner Kelly stated that Coppin actively provoked the officers and simulated holding a firearm.
  > *"The individual refused repeatedly to show his hands, kept his hand hidden under a garment, and made statements indicating he had a gun and intended to use it."*

* **On Coppin’s Statements to Officers:**
  According to police reports, Coppin yelled at the officers as he advanced toward them. Kelly quoted officers on the scene stating that Coppin shouted:
  > *"I have a gun! Shoot me! Shoot me! I’m not going back to the hospital!"*

* **On the Suicide Note:**
  Investigators recovered a handwritten note from Coppin’s pocket following the shooting, which police cited as evidence that he intended to provoke a lethal response from law enforcement ("suicide by cop"). Kelly read part of the note to the press:
  > *"I have a gun. I am going to shoot..."*

* **On the Hairbrush:**
  Addressing the revelation that Coppin was carrying a hairbrush, Kelly explained:
  > *"He had a black hairbrush inside his clothing, positioned in a way that led the officers to believe he was pointing a firearm at them. Officers on the scene were forced to make a split-second decision under the belief that their lives were in danger."*

---

### **Aftermath and Legal Outcome**

* **Public Outcry:** The incident sparked widespread protests led by civil rights advocates, including Rev. Al Sharpton, who argued that NYPD officers were improperly trained to handle individuals experiencing psychiatric crises and questioned why non-lethal options (such as Tasers) were not utilized.
* **Grand Jury Ruling:** In July 2008, a Brooklyn Grand Jury reviewed the evidence and testimony regarding the five officers involved. The grand jury declined to file criminal charges against the officers, concluding that their actions were legally justified based on the reasonable perception that Coppin posed an imminent deadly threat. 
* **City Settlement:** The NYPD subsequently instituted updates to its crisis intervention training, and the city later reached a financial settlement with Coppin's family.
